utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Tieger, yesterday, in the afternoon, we ended by some confusion. Could you tell us what the results of your research is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I will. It appeared that the most expeditious and effective way to resolve the problem from yesterday was simply to have the excerpts that would be presented to the Court correspond to the actual diary entries and to the pages, the sequential pages as they appear in the exhibit which has been provided broadly to the Court. So as near as I can determine, it was simply that the excerpted portions presented to the Court were miscopied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And they are now, as I understand it, presented to the Court in proper sequence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we can proceed without any further confusion. Then, Mr. Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just as I said yesterday that it would go without saying that you're still bound by your solemn declaration, the same is true for today. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Examined by Mr. Tieger: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, when we concluded yesterday, we were focusing on a diary entries from meeting of April 24th, 1993, which begins at ERN range R0164531. And I had just drawn your attention, if I recall correctly, to two entries on ERN page 4532, when we discovered some problems with the copying and numbering of the copies that had been provided to the Court. I think that problem has been resolved, so I'd like to return your attention now to that meeting and to a couple of entries from that meeting. And do you have page 4532 in front of you? I'd like to note two entries. One appears in the left side of the page, next to an asterisk. It's Dr. Karadzic speaking, and the entry notes: "We know that Kupres is vital for Croats, like Posavina for us. Before war we made a deal with Boban: Kupres/Posavina." And on the next page, next page of your diary but the same ERN page, it reflects Dr. Karadzic speaking again. And the entry notes: "What if Krajina Serbs gave land to Croatia for land to us in number 3?" Can you assist us, please, with what Dr. Karadzic is speaking about and what he's indicating about a deal with Boban or the proposition that the Krajina Serbs give land in Croatia in exchange for land to the Bosnian Serbs in the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was, as we know, unhappy with the Vance-Owen map. The Bosnian Serbs' leadership was all extremely unhappy. That has been established. So there was a good deal of suggested changes, or what we call in America horse-trading. And here he is suggesting a trade. But the trade was - excuse me - the trade was not in this case inside Bosnia necessarily. Perhaps the Krajina was the Bosnian Krajina, but maybe it was the Croatian Krajina, the old Vojna Krajina. It's hard -- I suspect -- it's hard to tell exactly whether he was talking about a trade inside or outside, because he says "... gave land to Croatia..." So presumably, you know, he's saying: Well, okay, we will give some of the western area, the western area of Bosnia, to Croatia for land given to us. You see, what if the Krajina Serbs gave land to Croatia to use in number 3? But number 3 - excuse me - province 3 was not in the west, so here he's talking about the Posavina. He's talking about the Posavina, province 3. In any case, it was an impossible idea. But he is suggesting that the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, would be willing to give some land to Croatia in exchange for other territories they got. Not something that could be accepted. And Lord Owen responds that these are separate issues and goes on to say: If you can do it informally, it's your business. The UNPAs, that is to say, the United Nations protected areas, are all separate in history, geography, and current status. And his reference to the UN protected areas clearly shows that Lord Owen took this to assume that Lord Owen inferred from what Karadzic said that they were talking about Croatia, because the UN protected areas were only in Croatia. So here you see Karadzic suggesting a trade of land in Bosnia for land in Croatia. And Lord Owen says that's impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me draw your attention very quickly, in the interests of time, to a couple of additional entries in that same meeting. I think they reflect issues that you've already covered in detail and it may well be that no comment is necessary. But if we turn to page R0164533, on the left side of the page, at the very top, there's an entry reflecting comments by MK, Mr. Krajisnik, which indicates: "Raises Sarajevo and suggests solutions for 'inner' 'outer' area." And then below that, after an indication that the map talk continues, there's an entry: "RM" - Ratko Mladic - "wants entire west bank of Drina (no way" - that's underscored - "colon, DLO/HSO)" that is Lord Owen and yourself. So do those two entries reflect again Mr. Krajisnik raising the question of the -- and the demand for the division of Sarajevo and General Mladic expressing the demand of the Bosnian Serb leadership for the entire area of the Drina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Mr. Krajisnik, as we mentioned repeatedly before, was intensely interested in dividing Sarajevo, and this was another example of that. And following that, I see we discussed Popovo Polje - that's down in the south-eastern section - and Nevesinje and Sarajevo again. And General Mladic said that they wanted -- the Bosnian Serbs wanted the entire bank of the Drina. We knew that, of course. I mean, they said that repeatedly and their actions in the Drina, the ethnic cleansing, made that clear. And we said no. Lord Owen and I said that was out of the question. The areas that were discussed probably most frequently, that is, insisted upon by the Bosnian Serb leadership consistently, persistently, were the Drina area, the west bank of the Drina, the corridor, and particularly Brcko, which is the choke point in the corridor, and Sarajevo. I would say among the areas, the territorial demands that they focused on, and these were constant, the three that were highlighted most, both in terms of the number of times we heard that and the depth of their insistence were the division of Sarajevo, gaining control of the entire west bank of the Drina, and Brcko, as the choke point in the corridor that we've discussed, the Posavina corridor. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, if I could quickly draw your attention to two additional meetings. The first is a meeting of the -- again of the 24th of April, 1993. That meeting begins on ERN page R0164535, and the particular entry to which I want to draw your attention is contained on the following page, at 4536. And that is a meeting involving yourself, Lord Owen, and President Cosic and President Milosevic. And again I think this is an issue you've covered in some depth earlier, so no comment may be necessary, but drawing your attention to an entry that appears toward the bottom right-hand portion of page 4536, Mr. Milosevic says: "C and I" - which I take to mean Cosic and I - "will talk this afternoon with Karadzic and Krajisnik Re Int. Presidency," and there's a word I cannot confidently decipher --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The word is "consensus" and "int." is interim. Interim Presidency and consensus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the passage continues: "We'll talk to K and K" - Karadzic and Krajisnik - "and have by end of day a clear understanding. We'll inform you. Maybe talk tomorrow." Again, Ambassador, is that another reflection of the understanding of President Milosevic and President Cosic regarding who the top two leaders of the Bosnian Serbs were?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no question in their minds or ours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Ambassador, if I could now draw your attention to a similar entry in your diary from a meeting of April 25th, 1993, found at ERN R0164553. This is a meeting which begins with President Cosic, President Milosevic, President Bulatovic, which Dr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik joined at 4.00 p.m., and the entry reads: "SM" - Slobodan Milosevic - "explains in our presence to Radovan Karadzic and Momcilo Krajisnik," indicated by initials, "where we stand on the MOU map on the interim arrangements." And I only draw your attention to that as another reflection of what you've previously indicated. Unless some comment is necessary, we'll move on to the next item.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would only mention, Mr. Tieger, that again we see reference to the corridor at the very bottom of page R0164536. On the lower right-hand side, at the bottom, President Milosevic says, yet again: "Regarding the map, the key is the corridor, the Posavina corridor." And he continues to say: "Please talk to Tudjman and Izetbegovic on this in province number 3." Because province number 3 was the mixed Croat-Muslim province that bordered on the Sava River and cut the corridor from Belgrade to Banja Luka. This again was the reference to that choke point at Brcko. And in this connection, I might mention that before the war, the opstina of Brcko had no ethnic majority. But of the three peoples who lived in Brcko, the minority were the Serbs. 80 per cent of the province was non-Serb -- of the population of Brcko, of Brcko opstina, in the pre-war census. It was approximately 40 per cent Muslim people, 30 per cent Croat people, and 20 per cent Bosnian Serbs. The exact figures are 39 per cent, 29, and 20. So, you see, one fifth of the province were Serb. 80 per cent or so of the people living in this opstina, according to the 1981 census, were non-Bosnian Serbs, were not Bosnian Serbs. They were either Bosnian Croats or Bosnian Muslims. Yet the Serbs insisted fiercely that this must become a Serb province - not an opstina but a province - in the Republika Srpska. Now, what was to happen to those other people? Because the pre-war population of the opstina of Brcko was over 80.000, which meant that about 60.000 or so were not Bosnian Serbs. Well, they were to be ethnically cleansed, as indeed they were. So that gives you an example, a clear one, of this Bosnian Serb insistence, absolute demand, and here you have Milosevic saying this is the key to an opstina that was not Serb. It was done, of course, for strategic reasons. That we knew. Everybody knew that. But what it involved was cleansing the area by force and violence of the other peoples who formed 80 per cent of the populace of that Brcko opstina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the record, the reference to which the ambassador referred, found at 4536, is a reference back to the meeting of April 24th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'd like now to show you a document which is shorthand notes from an enlarged session of the Council for Coordinating Positions on State Policy, which was held on the 21st of January of 1993. I know you've had an opportunity to look at that before. I think this is a -- this is a copy of the document to which you previously had access.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: With the Court's permission and permission of the Defence, which has already been indicated, I would provide this to the witness for his assistance in responding to the questions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, Ambassador, is it correct that this is a meeting that took place during the course of negotiations over the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The plan, as I mentioned earlier, was -- excuse me. The plan was put before the three parties in the first week of January, and this would be following on the initial discussions about the plan, which took about two weeks. They're all in my diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And have you had a chance to review this document and determine who the participants were and what the principal subject matter discussed was?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have had that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give the Court some idea who was in attendance and what principally they were discussing.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This coordinating committee meeting brought together about 20 or so, the top 20 political and military leadership of Yugoslavia, including Serbia and Montenegro, with the Bosnian Serb leadership. These are the most important decision-makers of the -- of those groups, that is to say, Yugoslavia, including Serbia, Montenegro, and the Bosnian Serbs. The top leadership.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the course of that meeting, what issue was focused on by those top leaders?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they discussed the entire Vance-Owen Plan. I would say the emphasis, as I recollect it from having glanced through it, was probably on two questions: On the territorial issue and on the ethnic issue. But all of the issues were covered, that is to say, the three aspects of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan, namely, the constitutional principles, the map, and the military agreements. They were all discussed quite thoroughly by the coordinating group. I note that the meeting lasted hours and hours. I think it's almost three hours. It begins at 5.10 p.m. and ends at 8.00, so it was basically a three-hour meeting. They covered the issues quite thoroughly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I draw your attention to a few passages --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I wonder, might I ask, is there a B/C/S version of this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is already in evidence. It was admitted during the course of Mr. Treanor's testimony, and yes, there is a B/C/S transcript available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar informs me that it's in P65, tab 220. Is that ...? 220 is perhaps ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say on a practical matter. I had a discussion with Mr. Harmon the other day about this. Your Honour may have noticed, so far as you thought about it, but it's not -- it's not the Defence practice at the moment to bring every exhibit into Court every day, because if we look at the volume of the Treanor material, in addition to everything else we have to do, carrying all this stuff backwards and forwards to and from Court just in case we should refer to a couple of documents, that really would be rather onerous. So it's only that on something like this we could no doubt find such material and bring it with us if we had an indication. But I hope that -- Mr. Harmon didn't indicate his expectation was necessarily that we should do that. Whatever has happened in other cases, because this case is rather heavier on documentation than many in relation to Mr. Treanor alone. So whatever the practice of other Defence teams, it's not intended, Your Honour, with respect, to be our practice to bring every exhibit in the case, and it's obviously going to increase as the case goes on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand, Mr. Stewart. On the other hand, but I don't know whether it was finally now distributed to you that the list of exhibits of the 22nd of June specifically mentions the -- I would say the Treanor exhibits that were intended to be used during the examination of the witness. So therefore, I do understand that you wouldn't take all of the, what was it, 18 binders, but at least there is a clear indication what you could expect. At least on this list. I have not consulted previous lists, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that would be terrific if we had that list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That would be a very helpful solution and pointer for us if we had that particular list that Your Honour is referring to, but we haven't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's the same -- it seems a failure to properly communicate with the other party on -- especially on the 22nd of June. I do not know whether on any previous list the exhibit already appears. We could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The original is here, so we could provide it to Mr. Krajisnik, but I know that Madam Registrar is always very concerned about the chain of custody, but I trust --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we entirely understand Madam Registrar's position. Our case manager takes the same approach. She requires an undertaking to give back to her a document, and we understand the practical reasons for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's make sure, Mr. Tieger. The 22nd of June list, of which we more or less established yesterday that it was not in the hands of - I'm not saying for what reason - has it been provided then or have you asked to be provided with a copy or additional copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of that list, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I've just asked a few moments ago, Your Honour, for the reason that that's the first time I was aware of its existence. So I don't have a practice, Your Honour, without being flippant, of asking for documents the existence of which I'm unaware of. That would be going rather far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's make sure that documents containing the -- well, the time estimate, six or eight hours, attached to it the exhibits to be shown, that they should always be in the hands of the other party in due time. That means well before the start of the examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears to me that the good news here is that we indeed have a procedure which is intended to cover this. Of course, the bad news is that there seems to have been some kind of mix-up in the course of executing that. I don't think either of us know at this point precisely what happened, but that is certainly something that we can address in future efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And finally, the good news is that this was the last time it would happen. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we solved the immediate practical problem. Thank you very much. We will hand back that document, of course, to Madam Registrar in due course. And I agree with what Mr. Tieger has just said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let us now return to the document itself. And I'd like to draw your attention to a few comments by participants in the meeting. The first of which are comments by Vladislav Jovanovic, which can be found at page 19 of the document. And during the course of his comments, Mr. Jovanovic states: "Therefore, the territorial link with Serbia and Montenegro, in other words, with Yugoslavia, has to be ensured in an undisputable way -- indisputable way which is not transitory. But, what is more important is to make the territory that we get, nationally homogenous as soon as possible, but not by means of ethnic cleansing and so on. Ethnic cleansings are palms off/as written/. So, we should use the peacetime process of the exchange of inhabitants, in other words migration and immigration, which will flow. What is important is that life in that future Bosnia becomes impossible and that everybody understands that individually, that they rush off to their original provinces. This is a strategic goal to which we should aspire and which should be achieved."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I understand that the interpreters -- I hope the interpreters have a copy of this. Nevertheless, I will, for their benefit, attempt to speak slower when referring to portions of the document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, first, can you shed any light on what Mr. Jovanovic is talking about and the extent to which it may have reflected positions taken during the course of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovanovic was the Yugoslav foreign minister at this period, and he says, correctly, that he has not been deeply involved in the negotiations with the Bosnian Serbs. That's what he means when he says, "I'm an amateur on the sidelines." What he's saying here is that the ethnic cleansing carried out by force and violence is hurting the Bosnian Serb cause internationally, which is surely the case. He knew that. That was evident. And he is therefore suggesting that the ethnic cleansing be carried out in a smoother fashion, as the counsel has just read.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, subsequent to Mr. Jovanovic's remarks, Dr. Karadzic speaks, on page 20 of the document, and the portion to which I'd like to draw your attention is contained toward the bottom of that page, where Dr. Karadzic states: "I think that this which Jovanovic is talking about, has already happened to a huge extent. There was fifty-fifty of us in Zvornik. The number of inhabitants of Zvornik is the now same, approximately 50.000, and they are all Serbs." And I'd also like to draw your attention to comments by Mr. Krajisnik on page 21 and 22. At the bottom of page 21, Mr. Krajisnik states: "Let me start with what Mr. Jovanovic was talking about, and Radovan was also talking in that direction. The problem is not 45 per cent of the territory and whether it will be 55 per cent. The part they now took from ethnically pure Serbian territories and gave to the others, that is the biggest resource we had in our territories." And there are further comments by Mr. Krajisnik contained on page 22, that it would be catastrophic to think about 45 per cent of territory, because it is not important how big the territory is in percentage, but what the quality of that territory is, and he discusses the need to seriously approach the issue of maps. And then states in the middle of the second-to-last paragraph on page 22: "We have to solve one part at a time. Something through politics, something else through migration, and some things through settlement, et cetera." Ambassador, again, any comments you have that may illuminate the issues being discussed by Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Jovanovic, and others, and the extent to which they may have been reflected in positions taken during the course of the Vance-Owen peace process?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they're entirely consistent with what they expressed to us at the negotiating table. They're discussing here ways to break up Yugoslavia, the need for the ethnic cleansing. You've seen at the beginning the first statement by Foreign Minister Jovanovic says, Don't do it so brutally, just take your time about it, let it happen. Make the place unlivable. Make certain areas unlivable so that the populations will move "voluntarily." Then Karadzic comes back, talking about Zvornik, he says, We've already ethnically cleansed Zvornik, you see. That's at the bottom of page 20. He says it used to be 50/50. Actually, plurality was Muslim. But anyway, Dr. Karadzic says it used to be 50/50. Now there are still 50.000 people in the opstina and they're all Serb. Meaning the other 50 per cent, the Muslims, have been cleansed. So that was Dr. Karadzic's response to the Jovanovic point about go easy on the ethnic cleansing because it's hurting you internationally. And Mr. Krajisnik takes another tack. He says the issue is not just the 45 per cent, because, as we mentioned yesterday, the Vance-Owen map, the Serb-majority provinces constituted 43 per cent of the territory. So he states it in an approximate fashion, nothing wrong with that. He says the problem is not 45 per cent of the territory or whether it will be 55 - remember that the claim of the Bosnian Serbs was always 65 - but he's complaining -- Mr. Krajisnik is, at the bottom of page 21, that the quality of the land -- the resources of the territories in that 43 per cent were insufficient. That made him unhappy. And he also notes that they're ethnically cleansed, by the way. I think the word "pure" probably in the original Serbo-Croatian was "clean" or "cleansed." "Cistiti." I would assume it was "cistiti" or some variant of "cistiti". And then on page 22, Mr. Krajisnik continues in the same vein, giving examples of the resources that he believed were taken from the Bosnian Serbs and given to the other communities. And he states it quite frankly. He says: We have to think of the quality of the land we have, not just the size. So for Mr. Krajisnik, the question here was both quantity, how much land the Bosnian Serbs would take, and how much they would assume was theirs, therefore; and also the quality of that land. And he felt that they had been treated badly by the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Finally, Ambassador, let me direct your attention to comments by Nikola Koljevic, and those are contained at the bottom of page 24 and the top of page 25. Dr. Koljevic states: "We will have to organise huge political activity in order to win people over this for this --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me, forgive me for interrupting, but in the last answer, the witness speculated about what the original Serbo-Croat, Croatian, was his phrase, said. Rather than leave this to be sorted out in hours' time, it seems appropriate -- after all, the witness is not, as I understand it, qualified, he's speculating that that's what it might say. We can clear that up straight away, I suggest, and then it's more neatly on the same passage of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the words you expressed in Serbo-Croatian. Because you referred to language they use. So it can be translated to us in English. But it was in my mind that these were varieties of the word "clean."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I said I assumed that the "pure" here was "cistiti" in some form. The interpreters can tell us that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could they tell us what "cistiti" is, if I pronounce it well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Cleanse," or "clean."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't hear what they said, Your Honour. What did they say? What was the answer?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They said -- you are on what channel at this moment? Because if --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm hearing you in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please check whether Mr. Okun is on channel 4 or channel 0 perhaps. You're now on 4. That means whenever someone speaks another language it will be translated to you in English. But until now, English has been the prevailing language. So they -- their translation was "cleanse" or "clean."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So I was correct in my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you for clearing that up, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm not quite sure this deals with the point. The witness was speculating as to what the original word in Serbian or Serbo-Croat, B/C/S, what the original word was. I'm suggesting we can clear up what the original word was, and then -- if we simply work in English we're just going to be endlessly repeating what the witness has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm certainly prepared to put the Serbian on the ELMO and we can check right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe that's what counsel is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, it seems to be sensible to do it right now rather than have two disjointed bits of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put it on the ELMO. I misunderstood your observation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps I didn't make myself sufficiently clear, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if I may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In English, we see President Cosic saying, "Momcilo Krajisnik, you are next," and in the B/C/S we see that passage: "Momcilo Krajisnik izvolite," and then Mr. Krajisnik begins to speak. You can see the reference to 45 and 55, as you do in the English and in the B/C/S, and then you can see in the next sentence, and you may want to have the language staff interpret it, but you can clearly see the words "etnicko ciscenje Srpska teritorija."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the language originally used. Do we still need to have the four words translated or is it clear enough now?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I had better say what I understand the position to be and then we can confer. Because after all, I have the big advantage of having Ms. Cmeric with me. What I'm informed is that "cistiti" there, it's the equivalent, if you like, of "clean" or "pure," but it is not the equivalent as a grammatically -- of "cleaned" or "cleansed." In other words, it's not the verb form, it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not the verb in its perfect form, but -- you mean something can be clean without being cleansed just before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I rather do mean that, Your Honour, because that's clearly so. The thrust of the witness's evidence, I think, was that the original Serbo-Croat would -- he was speculating was "cleansed" or "cleaned" [Realtime transcript read in error "clean"]. Perhaps he said "cleansed." It's -- well, I've made the point, Your Honour. There's nothing more for me to say on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point is clear. It's a matter of interpretation of language, and we now have -- you've drawn our attention to the fact that, at least in the view of the Defence, several interpretations are possible, not exactly being the same. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's return, then, to the comments by Mr. Koljevic -- Dr. Koljevic, please. And Ambassador, I was drawing your attention to the comment by Dr. Koljevic that begins at the bottom of page 24: "We will have to organise huge political activity in order to win people over for this, and we will have to develop the activity of settlement homogenisation while there's still time."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. Could I -- I'm sorry to interrupt again, but on the transcript, in my last observation - and this would just cause confusion in future, I used the phrase -- this is at 9:54:50. He was speculating -- I said I think that the original Serbo-Croat, what he was speculating was "cleansed" or 'clean.' Your Honour, I'm pretty sure I said "cleaned." And if that remains on the transcript as "clean" instead of "cleaned," that's going to utterly confuse the point I was making because the whole point was to be drawing a distinction between "clean" as an adjective and "cleaned" as a verb form. So if that isn't corrected, that would simply make further confusion of what I've said. Perhaps I could just note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you said "clean." Is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The point was what I said, Your Honour. Because if I'm recorded as having said "clean" there, when I believe I said "cleaned," it doesn't make much sense, in the end, of what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I fully understand. You made your point quite clear now. And I -- it's off my screen now. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No doubt this is all crystal clear in the B/C/S translation to anybody listening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The point is perfectly clear to us at this moment. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, I'm not going to read Dr. Koljevic's remarks again, but bearing in mind the remarks that preceded it and Dr. Koljevic's comments about the need to develop the activity of settlement homogenisation while there's still time, can you comment, please, about Dr. Koljevic's remarks in the context of that meeting and the extent to which that position was reflected and positions taken by the Bosnian Serb leadership during the course of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is also consistent. Mr. Koljevic's remarks are consistent with the Bosnian-Serbs' ethnic cleansing, that is to say, the desire to achieve ethnically clean provinces, as Dr. Karadzic gave the example. And we have a specific example in front of us at this meeting where Dr. Karadzic speaks about Zvornik, where he says it used to be 50/50, but now it's 100 per cent Serb. And this is what Koljevic is referring to as "settlement homogenisation."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. I'd like to present you now with a portion of the transcript from the 34th Assembly Session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, which was held in the latter part of 1993 over the course of several days, 27th to the 29th of August, 9th and 10th of September, and the 29th through the 1st of October 1993. And Ambassador, in particular, I'd like to draw your attention to an exchange between a delegate by the name of Rajko Kasagic and Mr. Krajisnik, which appears beginning page 47 and continues on to page 48. And to quickly give the context, or at least to paraphrase Mr. Kasagic --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could I take a moment to read it? I'm seeing this for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to set the -- I want to draw your attention to a particular comment by Mr. Krajisnik, but I want to put it in appropriate context. Is it correct that Mr. Kasagic raises concerns about the problem with whether or not the Bosnian Serbs will get a corridor, and then suggests the possibility of giving Sarajevo away, in his words, "So let's give that Sarajevo away and let's charge for it as much as it is worth."

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The speaker, Rajko Kasagic, emphasises strongly the importance of Brcko, that is to say, the choke point in the corridor, and says, in effect, quite directly, in fact, he is suggesting a trading Sarajevo, the Serb position in Sarajevo, for acquiring a firm Serb position in Brcko. And Mr. Krajisnik reacts negatively to that proposal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik states in part, and that can be -- that sentence can be found in approximately the middle of the paragraph that appears on page 48: "Let me tell you, gentlemen: Muslims and Croats ask for their municipality in Banja Luka, which we did not accept because we must have that territory clean." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is that response by Mr. Krajisnik and the position he takes in response to Mr. Kasagic's remarks consistent with the positions he took during the course of the Vance-Owen peace process?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to clarify: Did peace discussions, peace negotiations, or efforts toward a resolution of the conflict continue after the rejection of the Vance-Owen Peace Plan by the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Other negotiators continued and other plans and maps were proposed to the party. At this period, the August/September 1993 period, the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia was continuing, under the chairmanship of Lord Owen for the EC, and Thorvald Stoltenberg, who replaced Secretary Vance for the UN, and they developed other maps to put before the parties, and other arrangements. This end of August/September was the period when the so-called Invincible Plan was being discussed, named Invincible because the parties met on a British warship in the Adriatic, with the name Invincible, and so the discussions and the map and the documents that came out of that meeting were referred to as "the Invincible Plan" in the fall of 1993. At approximately the same period, but a bit later, Presidents Milosevic and Tudjman together proposed a plan which was called "the Tudjman-Milosevic Plan." And then somewhat later, but beginning in 1993, the contact group, consisting of the six countries that formed it, developed a map which they presented in July 1994. This period, August/September 1993, focused mostly on the Invincible map discussions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me next draw your attention, if I may, and present you with a portion of the 37th Session of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, held on January 10th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just in order to make it possible for those who will later read the transcript to retrieve the documents, I'd like to invite Madam Registrar to tell us under what number the exhibit we last have discussed was admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It was Exhibit P65, tab 221.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this particular document falls within the same general category. It's also a P65 document. However, my list, although it did contain the tab number for the previous document, does not contain the tab number under which this document was previously submitted. But as indicated, it is a P65 document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- it's a P65 document. But to ask people to go through 18 binders is -- so if you could clarify that which -- under which tab those minutes are to be found, that would certainly assist those who have to struggle through these transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, let me draw your attention to comments by Mr. Krajisnik, which are contained on page 4 of the translation that's in front of you, in the second paragraph, in which Mr. Krajisnik states: "Believe me that the biggest tragedy would be if the Muslims agreed to live together with us. You saw how they were squeezing in the Croats, but the Croats do not want it. We would lose our state. That is the only thing that I would not accept. I would accept, however, that we be granted a smaller percentage of territory than we have now, provided that we remain separated and that we have our own state without Muslims."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, if I may interrupt. Again it is about numbering. I see that this document starts with page 1 out of 153, then page 2 out of 153, and then the next page is 1 out of 5, which is at least surprising. I'm not asking you if you say this is -- if I look at the ERN numbers, I -- no. There are ET numbers on top of it. And the first page and the second page have the same ET numbers, which suggests that it's the same document, whereas the third page and the fourth page and all the remaining pages have a different number on the top, which also surprises, because it seems that the top numbering is about documents and the bottom is about pages. And it's really confusing. I'm not saying that it's not the same document, but at least it raises some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I recall correctly, this matter was raised during the course -- when we had documents admitted following Mr. Treanor's testimony. I believe this is clearly the same exhibit. I think -- and first of all, let me indicate for the record, this is P65, tab 222.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And as we indicated at that time, this apparent discrepancy arose from the fact that portions of that particular session were translated. It wasn't translated in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If we discussed it at that time, I apologise for not having this clearly in my mind, every detail of the 18 binders. Well, the only thing that is at least promising is that the same inconsistencies in numbering are raised consistently, then and now again. Please -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was going to make, in slightly ironic form, the same apology, because the expectation sometimes for recollection of these things is beyond human ability.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Perhaps I should leave the irony to the parties. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, having in mind the comments by Mr. Krajisnik which I read out a few moments ago, can you tell us whether or not those comments are consistent with the positions taken by Mr. Krajisnik and the other Bosnian Serb leaders during the course of the Vance-Owen peace process negotiations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This comment from January 10, 1994 is consistent with the positions taken by the Bosnian Serb leadership and Mr. Krajisnik, as the -- one of the leaders during the Vance-Owen discussions, and it's also consistent with the document we just looked at from January 21st, 1993, particularly this remark fully consistent with the earlier ones of Dr. - excuse me - Mr. Krajisnik: "I would accept, however, that we, that is, the Bosnian Serbs, Republika Srpska, that we be granted a smaller percentage of territory than we now have, provided that we remain separated and that we have our own state without Muslims." Well, that's quite consistent with everything we heard, the need for the state, the ethnic purity, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, Ambassador, I'd like you to -- or I'd like to draw your attention to a video clip that has been previously shown to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is P70, Your Honour, and the transcript, I think, is P70.1 or P70.1A. Now that the transcripts have all been distributed, I'd ask that the video be played.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, the video --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a transcript problem at this moment, Mr. Tieger, because the -- we have a written English text, but the translation does not appear in the transcript. I'll deal with the matter during the next break. Let's proceed at this moment. We have had this problem before, and I just would like to find out how we solved it at that time. But at least it's on the record now that there is a problem. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, may I have your comments, please, on the presentation by Mr. Krajisnik contained in the video.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could I just ask, Your Honour. I'm not quite sure -- again, if it was said weeks and weeks and weeks ago, I just forget, whether we actually had a date for this videotape. Because the transcript doesn't show one. It says 1992. I don't know whether it was identified previously as being for a more specific date.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We -- the question was raised. The answer is there is not a specific date, but a range. But I'll be more than happy to ask the ambassador if he can place -- assist us in identifying the approximate date by virtue of the comments made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, if you can incorporate that in your remarks.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can answer that. It's clear from the internal evidence of the remarks that the map that Mr. Krajisnik was using in this video was something that would have been available to him and that he says was shown in Geneva between September and December. Why do I say that? Because of the lay of the land, that is, how much the Serb forces had conquered, the battle line that he showed on the map. That's point one. The second point is he says our people offered this in Geneva. And this would have been during the International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, which met in Geneva. And the fact that he doesn't mention at all the Vance-Owen maps which were put down in January leads me to conclude that this discussion, his graphic description of this map and what it stood for and what the Bosnian Serb goals were, occurred sometime between December and December [sic] 1992. As to his description of the situation and the two maps, the overlay and the ethnic map under it, this is consistent with the Bosnian Serb position. He refers to the need to retain the Drina, the corridor, the need for ethnically pure Serb, or clean, or cleansed, whichever semantic word you choose. He emphasises the Sarajevo question again. But the problem with his presentation is when he lifts the overlay, the transparent overlay, which showed the front line, the battle lines, that 70 per cent of the territory held by the VRS, the Bosnian Serb army and their territorials, because the map underneath that, which Mr. Krajisnik says is consistent with the battle line, is by no means consistent with the battle line. In fact, it's quite inconsistent. Because the territory he claimed on the transparency showed the Serbs occupying the entire Drina, west bank, up to the Neretva River, that huge swath along the Drina. And as we all know, this area of the Drina - there were many, many Muslim opstinas on the Drina: Zvornik, Visegrad, et cetera. I mean, the ethnic maps are quite clear on that. And on the area in the western section, the Cazinska Krajina, the so-called Bihac pocket, he notes that the Una River is the border, and claims that this is consistent with the ethnic situation before the war, that is, before the ethnic cleansing. And that's not true. That's simply not true. There were Muslim plurality opstinas east of the Una River. Any ethnic map based on the census of 1981 or 1991 will show that. So that his assertion that the battle lines corresponded to the ethnic situation before the war is totally untrue, as a glance at the map will show.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I'm looking at the clock, and perhaps we could decide the issue of the transcript right away. But perhaps we should not bother Mr. Okun with this matter. Mr. Okun, we'll resume in 25 minutes. So if you could please be back then again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I mention. There was just a slip of the tongue in the very last answer. The witness at some point said "December to December 1992." It's quite clear from earlier in the answer that he meant September to December 1992, but it's as well to correct these things straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear to everyone. Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Okun out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I suggest that immediately after the break we play the same video again. It takes three minutes. The main problem is that the French transcript will not be the same as the English transcript any more. Do the interpreters have the English translation of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, they do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have. So let's then play it immediately after the break and have it translated in both the two official languages of the Tribunal. We adjourn until 5 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, the Chamber has decided, for technical reasons, to replay the video, but you don't have to answer the questions again about it. It's just to have the English translation of the video in the transcript. Mr. Tieger, let's proceed with the two minutes, 51 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we stop. Could we stop again. Yes. I'd like the interpreters to give the translation on the English channel which will result in the English text to appear in the transcript later on. Yes. Could you please restart.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Serbian people in the former Bosnia and Herzegovina. Momcilo Krajisnik speaking: "We are standing in front of the ethnic map of former Bosnia-Herzegovina, with marked borders of the territory presently held by the Bosnian Serb army. I can only say that what was being said, that we are holding territories ethnically populated by other national communities, is not true, which can be seen on the ethnic map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which we see covered with a transparent sheet, where our territories are exactly marked, and it is clearly seen that these are the territories that belong to our people. Such a map, similar to this, as far as I'm informed, was offered in Geneva and it was made clear that the Serbs want that the border of our country be here, that is, the Neretva River valley, and this is mostly the territory of the Bosnian Serb Republic, with the proviso that we allow that certain enclaves in our territory be populated by other ethnic communities. Sarajevo is a separate problem. It is marked here. The city proper is marked as Muslim territory, but we shall plead for demilitarisation and division between the two national communities, primarily the Serb and the Muslim ones, and maybe a municipality populated by Croats. The territory of the Bosnian Serb Republic represents in fact the border along the River Una, the River Sava, with a smaller area that is not yet under our forces. I mean it's not liberated yet. That is Orasje, the area of Semberija, the territory of Ozren and the territory of Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina. We presented as our territory to the Croatian community in Graz that our border should be between our two national communities that would be the Neretva River. In any case, this continuity of our territory is in one piece, so to speak, and we advocate that it be one constitutive unit of the Bosnian Serb Republic, and we allow the possibility that there be also constitutive units of the Bosnian Croat Republic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The beginning and the end is, as far as translation is concerned, seems to be a bit different from what we see on paper. The introduction what the presenter introduces is not fully translated. Is there any need to have that replayed and have that -- that is that: "Today, the president of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, Momcilo Krajisnik, showed to our reporter," et cetera. Do we have to play that? No. I see no need for that. And I noticed that at the very end, the translation was a bit different orally from what we see on paper. If the Defence would like to come back to that at a later stage, perhaps you could compare first and see whether it's of any importance to come back to that. We'll then now proceed. Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, the overlay used by Mr. Krajisnik shows a wide swath of territory west of the Drina which is claimed by the Bosnian Serbs and which Mr. Krajisnik says are those areas that belong to "our people." Does that area shown in the overlay correspond to the pre-war demographics of that area of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In part, yes; in part, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And looking at P273, the map that is to your left at this moment, does that map show the composition of the Drina area where the conflict began?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The areas of green are the areas of Muslim majority or plurality in those opstinas?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The green are Muslim plurality or majority opstinas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those are areas that were indeed ethnically populated by Muslims before the war began; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ambassador, unless you have any further comments on the video presentation, I will conclude my questions.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd like to make one or two brief comments on Mr. Krajisnik's television presentation. One notes at the very beginning of his presentation that he states that "We are standing in front of an ethnic map of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina." Well, as we've established, this map probably was being shown in the period September to December of 1992, and at that time, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a recognised state and member of the United Nations, and yet Mr. Krajisnik refers to it as the "former" Bosnia and Herzegovina, that is to say, he negates and denies the existence. And this statement that "We possess territories that were populated by other national communities" is not true. Well, that's an inaccurate statement. We can see the ethnic map. There is also -- it is also worth noting his statement about Orasje, that is, the opstina at the Posavina, which he says "They have not yet taken." If I could find that in the -- in his remarks. Yes. It's about three quarters of the way down in the English, where he says: "Territory of the Bosnian Serb Republic represents in fact the border along Una River, Sava River, with smaller area that is not yet under our forces, I mean it's not liberated yet." In other words, he was indicating that there were a few areas yet to be conquered militarily by the Bosnian Serb forces. He was quite frank about that. And again, that emphasises the importance that the Bosnian Serb leaders attached to the corridor, to the Posavina corridor, linking Belgrade through Brcko to Banja Luka. And he emphasises the continuity of the Bosnian Serb territories as then held by the Bosnian Serb armed forces. So what he's doing here is comparing the six strategic objectives of May 12, 1992 with the situation as actually existent at the time he was looking at the map, somewhere between September and December 1992. And one notices that he focuses on the principal points of the geography. And he is, in effect, saying, although he does not state it explicitly: We have achieved our aims, with the exception of Sarajevo. Because if you compare the war aims of May 1992 with this presentation, one sees that he discusses very carefully, very accurately, the war aims, the strategic objectives, with the situation as it existed on that map; the Una, the Neretva, the corridor, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, subject to the small physical --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The lectern is not common property, but in common use between the parties. Mr. Okun, you will be cross-examined by Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Stewart:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Mr. Stewart, would you kindly put your microphone on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just done it. Thank you. My microphone is on. Can you hear me? No answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, we can. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, the -- you described how the Carrington Peace Plan for the entire Yugoslavia was accepted by everybody except Serbia, and that meant, another way of phrasing it, is to say everybody except Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that a question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Is that -- would that -- is that an equally fair way of expressing it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say the Serb leadership. I don't know that one would ascribe 100 per cent of that rejection to President Milosevic. There were other leaders. Kontic was there. And it was the rejection by the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was the nub of their objection?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't think it was a fair solution to the problem, the position of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, in the fall of 1991 - this was the period we're discussing -- this was October 1991, to be specific. The position was that Yugoslavia was one country and that the declared independence of Croatia and Slovenia were illegal secessionary movements. So they didn't accept that position, and they had other arguments as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, of course the position they didn't accept what had happened, the Carrington Peace Plan, like every other plan looking forward, looking ahead to see how it could be resolved. What do you say were the key objections by the -- by Serbia to the Carrington Peace Plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had many objections. I perhaps would point particularly to the minority provisions in what was called chapter 2, in the second section of the Carrington elements of agreement. These were detailed provisions concerning the treatment of minorities in the various republics, and with specific reference to the question of ethnic Serbs living in Croatia, the Serb delegation to the Conference on Yugoslavia felt that they were not adequately treated in the Carrington plan. And at that point, it has to be noted, that Croatia had not fully accepted the second chapter. So among their other objections was that they were worried about the future of the Serb people in Croatia. I should mention that the Serb minority in Croatia constituted approximately 12 per cent of the overall population. 12 per cent of the Croatian population were Serbian, Orthodox Serbs. That was probably their principal objection.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there are two points particularly come out of that. First of all, you indicated that although -- your evidence was that the peace plan was in fact accepted by five of the six republics, that's subject to the qualification you've just mentioned then, that Croatia didn't fully accept every element of the peace plan as it was being propounded.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They accepted it. There was still some residual discussion of the second chapter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in a nutshell, then, at the time when Serbia made it clear that they did not agree, there would still have been further ground to cover and further elements to resolve?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true. Although the elements were not major in terms of the conference. Lord Carrington did not regard them as in any sense problems that could not be overcome. They were overcome. Croatia did accept the second chapter, very shortly. So it was really more a question of timing rather than overall acceptance. But Serbia never accepted any aspect of the Carrington proposals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the concern about the Serb minority in Croatia, it wasn't by any means an irrational concern, was it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you talked about the Badinter Commission, which reported - do you recall this would be right - sometime in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Badinter Commission issued decisions throughout this period, not just in January 1992. In December, for example, if I may, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In December, for example, coming back to your earlier question of the Yugoslav objections to the Carrington proposals, one of the principal Yugoslav points, as I mentioned, but it needs to be reiterated because it was the basis of their position, one of their principal points was that Yugoslavia existed; it was a country and there was an illegal rebellion against, an illegal secession against this country. So Lord Carrington asked the Badinter Commission to answer that question, and in December of 1991, the Badinter Commission did issue an avis, a decision on particularly that point. And what that commission decided was that Yugoslavia at that point was in a process of dissolution, that it was not, in fact, a coherent state any longer. And they said it was "dans un processus de dissolution" and that decision, needless to say, did not please the Yugoslav authorities. So they issued many decisions throughout the conference period, not just in January, although the one in January concerning recognition was a very important avis.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it right the Badinter Commission recommendation was that only Slovenia and Macedonia satisfied what were regarded as the appropriate conditions for independence and recognition of independence?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was recognition by the EC. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not by the rest of the world, of course. The Badinter Commission was speaking for the European Community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. It was an EC organ, wasn't it, effectively?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Yes. So that's exactly correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I think as far as Macedonia was concerned, well, Greece were an issue. Greece objected --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- to the position on Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And they had a veto on that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And vetoed. But it follows, doesn't it, as an obvious corollary, that since only Slovenia and Macedonia satisfied conditions for independence, the other republics, including, of course, Bosnia and Herzegovina, didn't?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did that relate -- well, particularly including issues such as satisfactory provisions to ensure the position of minorities within the republics concerned?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not directly. What they said in the decision was that there had not been an expression of will, in essence, that there needed to be some more of an expression of will within Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was correct, wasn't it, in effect? Well, it was their decision, but it wasn't a decision that serious commentators could challenge.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Well, the expectation was that, again by commentators at the period, was that a referendum would probably be held in Bosnia. That was the widespread expectation, in the wake of the Badinter Commission's decision, and in fact that happened, the next month. A referendum was held on February 29 and March 1, 1992. 1992, Your Honours, being a leap year, which explains February 29. It was held on a Saturday, February 29th, and Sunday, March 1, 1992. And that was held expressly, although implicitly, but expressly to satisfy that condition, if you will, expressed by the Badinter Commission of arbitration, an expression of will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The political pressures at this stage involving, weren't they, the European Community, particularly under a lot of pressure from Germany, to recognise Croatia, notwithstanding what Badinter had to say about the position?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, very much so. The Germans had made that clear. In fact, they had said in December that they were going to recognise Croatia by Christmas of 1991, regardless of what anybody else did or said. And this was opposed by other people. It was -- what Secretary Vance did, for example, as Secretary-General of the United Nations, wrote to Mr. van den Broek, who was then -- well, he was then the Dutch foreign minister and the Dutch were holding the Presidency of the community. And in December of 1991, the Secretary-General of the United Nations, Mr. Perez de Cuellar wrote a letter to him recommending that recognition not be granted piecemeal, that it be a coordinated, coherent act. And it was precisely around the issue of German -- the German desire to recognise Croatia immediately. And indeed, the letter that the Secretary-General of the United Nations wrote to Mr. van den Broek was answered by foreign minister Genscher of Germany. Not by van den Broek but by Genscher. So you're quite correct, Mr. Stewart, that the issue in December 1991, the issue of, shall we say, premature recognition of the seceding republics, was an issue very much in Lord Carrington's mind and very much an issue in front of the Conference on Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Genscher particularly, for Germany, he was their foreign minister, Mr. Genscher pushed extremely hard, didn't he, and eventually was successful in pushing the European Community on Croatia?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he pushed extremely hard. The degree of his success was, I think, limited, because in fact the European Community did not recognise until they received the decision from Mr. Badinter and the judges on his commission. And it was in connection with that chapter 2 that we mentioned earlier, the second chapter on minorities in the Carrington proposals of October 1991, that the issue was joined. Croatia did accept and implement the minority provisions. That removed the last bar to recognition of Croatia, and so the European Community did recognise. But there was no question that Germany pushed very hard for the earliest possible recognition of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's also true, isn't it, that Lord Carrington was not pleased and not happy about that approach.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. In fact, he also wrote to Mr. van den Broek in December on that point. I believe it was December 2nd, 1991, his letter to van den Broek. But of course it can be checked. It's a public letter in the public domain, as are the Secretary-General's letters. He wrote -- even before the Secretary-General wrote to van den Broek, Lord Carrington wrote to van den Broek, opposing early, premature recognition of one republic. And the reason why he did that, of course, was quite clear: He was working on an overall settlement for all of Yugoslavia. If one recognised Croatia at that point before the settlement were achieved, what incentive would the Republic of Croatia have to continue negotiating? It would have removed the pressure, if you will, of recognition. And that was the burden of Lord Carrington's argument in his letter to Mr. van den Broek of early December 1991. Yes, he opposed it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the sum of the basic political realities here were these, weren't they: That it was increasingly apparent that -- certainly if Croatia was heading for recognition of independence, so was Slovenia. That was very clear, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was clear. Slovenia, indeed, was the first country to declare its independence, and by this time, de facto, was independent. Because, as we know, the JNA, the Yugoslav People's Army, went into Slovenia in force in June 1991, ostensibly to protect their international border with Austria, in fact to suppress the independence, but within a week of fighting, they withdrew - I should say after a week of fighting, they withdrew - and never went back. So that was the situation in Slovenia as of the end of June 1991. So by December, Slovenia had been de facto independent for six months. That was not the case in Croatia, of course, where the JNA was involved in heavy fighting, heavy fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it fair to say in a nutshell that Slovenia didn't -- it didn't present the same intractable problems as Croatia and also, of course, Bosnia and Herzegovina; it was, in terms of its population, in terms of nationalities, it was nowhere near as difficult or complex as those republics?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that's surely the case. It's 90 -- I suppose over 90 per cent Slovenian, probably over 95 per cent Slovenian in population. The second group, there were some pockets. There were some Croats and Italians, of course. I mean, there were many Italians in Slovenia since portions of Slovenia had been in Italy. But yes, you're correct that it was ethnically -- Slovenia is Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the problem with Slovenia and independence was more that it was -- it was the start of the very process of dissolution that the Badinter Commission were referring to then in the terms that you described.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's part of the problem. The other issue which was very important in Slovenia is the wealth of the republic. Slovenia, with a population that in pre-war constituted about 8 per cent of the overall population of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, that is, the pre-war population, with that 8 per cent, they produced about one quarter of the gross national product of the country. So economically, it was very important. But ethnically it did not present the same challenges.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But then looking at those developments in late 1991 and early 1992, from the position of Serbs, and whether in Croatia or in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or indeed in Serbia, the -- Slovenia and Croatia appeared to be heading quite firmly and quickly towards recognition of independence. That's -- we seem to be agreed on that so far.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was, by the end of 1991, also already clear that Mr. Izetbegovic in Bosnia-Herzegovina and his colleagues also had in mind independence for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both Macedonia and Bosnia and Herzegovina had also declared their independence before the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that from the point of view of the Bosnian Serbs, a lot of the writing was on the wall as to where things were going, wasn't it? Perhaps I'll be more specific: They clearly were going to find it already difficult to the point of impossible in the long run to resist the progress towards independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that it would have been a reasonable assumption to believe that the four republics would all become independent one day, that -- and receive recognition; that Croatia -- that Slovenia and Croatia would be the first and that the others would follow. I think that was reasonable, yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's also correct, isn't it, that if that was likely to follow in the way that you have acknowledged, it was very specifically something that the Bosnian Serbs did not want and would not have wanted to see happen?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we know they opposed it. They vigorously and violently opposed it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So that in the negotiations -- now, the position was this, wasn't it: You said the Dutch had the Presidency for the second half of 1991, of the European Community. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Portugal took over from the 1st of January; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's how Mr. Cutilheiro came into it. He was invited then to take over in the way that you've described.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so the Serbs were --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Stewart. I'm seeing Mr. Cutileiro's name misspelled on my monitor. There is no "H" in the middle of his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The transcript will be reviewed over night in order to get all the names as they should be. That sometimes causes a problem. Thank you very much. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's Cutileiro, not Cutilheiro.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I expect Mr. Cutileiro probably suffers from being one of the most misspelled people around.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anyway, the gentleman from Portugal, Mr. Cutileiro, he took over specifically in relation to Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you have described. The Bosnian Serbs were, right from the very beginning of the Cutileiro process, if I can call it that, were engaged in something in a negotiation based on a fundamental point that they didn't like but, for practical purposes, were being driven to accept for the purpose of those negotiations, Bosnia and Herzegovina as a separate state.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's partially correct. I would not say they were being driven to accept Bosnia-Herzegovina by the negotiations. Bosnia-Herzegovina was about to be, as we've indicated earlier, an independent, recognised state and member of the international community. So it was not the negotiations that were accomplishing that. That was the decision of the international community. After all, one has to be voted in to the General Assembly of the United Nations. It's not automatic, you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So that was the situation. But -- and that they recognised was likely to happen. What they wanted was to have their own state, their own entity, under the umbrella, and that they declared, even before Bosnia was recognised, as we've discussed several days ago, they, already in November, December, and January - that is, November and December 1991 and January 1992 - they took steps to establish what they saw as the Republika Srpska.
