I mean, they proclaimed it in existence in January. They issued a constitution in February. But they understood it would be under a -- what they hoped would be a fictional Bosnian state, or a nominal state, so weak as not to affect their interests.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Okun, I think we can, in the light of your answer, we can agree that if we take away "by the negotiations," the context was that the real world, the political forces, were driving in that direction?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the Cutileiro meetings and discussions led to the -- particularly to the two agreements, which were effectively in two stages that we've mentioned. There was first Lisbon and then Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Excuse me. There were also referred to at that time "London Agreements," because they met in London from time to time to accommodate Lord Carrington's interest and his presence in London. So it was rather movable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was a continuing process, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the two key documents that emerged from this, for our purposes, could be regarded as the Lisbon Agreement and the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you ask Cutileiro and Lord Carrington, they would say London and Lisbon. And I'm sorry, but that's what they say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's helpful to know what they would say if they were and were asked.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the essence is, I think, rather look at the documents than worry about the location.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because, as you say correctly, it was a continuing process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the two documents, the Lisbon Agreement, as we call it, and the Sarajevo Agreement, are exhibits already in this case. We've looked at them before. D5 and D6. I think it might be helpful -- they're not very large documents. It might be helpful, Mr. Okun, if you could be given both.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have the copy I was given previously.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would do fine, Mr. Okun. Well, it seems it may not do fine. I'd better check.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I have is entitled 02093996, 15-XI-00. The 11 is in Roman numerals. And on the front page it says "Regards, Jose Cutileiro." It was obviously given to somebody by Ambassador Cutileiro. Yes. It's what I have. Thank you. I have it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Okun. In fact, as often happens in this case, D6 and D5, D6 comes chronologically first. That's the Lisbon Agreement. We think that was around 27th of February, 1992. Whether that's the exact date -- it was late February, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not directly involved. It would have been February and March, I believe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the Sarajevo Agreement, that's D5, that actually has the date 18th March 1992.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. It was February, March, and, as you say, it was a continuum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And if we look particularly, if we take D6, that's the other document to the one that you specifically referred to a moment ago, the general principles -- well, independence. It starts with A. I'll try and pick out the pertinent points and not grind through all the text. But Bosnia and Herzegovina, independence is the first section. It would, after independence, be an independent state composed of three constituent units. And then number 3, the people of the three nations, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, would realise their sovereign rights through the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And then it sets out constitutional principles, many of which would be widely regarded as unobjectionable, as elements of a constitution. I don't think we need dwell in detail on those. And then there's a provision for assembly and government. And then D, the constituent units. Number 1, within Bosnia and Herzegovina, three constituent units would be established, whose territory would be those envisaged in part E below. And that's where I want to go next, please, Mr. Okun, part E, definition of the constituent units. The territory of the constituent units would be defined on the basis of the -- and then it's left open, 1971, 1981, or 1991 census, and the existing communes, with only such small adjustments as may be clearly justified in such a way that communes where one particular nation is clearly in a majority are grouped together into the appropriate constituent unit. And then a state may have several separate parts. If there are any particular areas, difficulties of definition remain, the assistance of the arbitration commission would be requested. And was that Mr. Badinter's commission?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Sarajevo would be the capital. Now, then if we -- this is, as you've confirmed, this, of course, was a continuing process. If we look, then, at the Sarajevo Agreement, so it's coming just a few weeks later, it's been refined, of course, as one would expect. Lots of gaps have been filled and some of the choices that were left open in the first draft have been made effectively by the drafters of the second document, the Sarajevo Agreement. And in particular, if we look at the constituent units -- I won't dwell on A, B, and C. Look at the constituent units D1, within Bosnia and Herzegovina, constituent units would be established which are defined in part E below. Then we get the definition: "A Working Group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographical, and other criteria. A map based on the national, absolute, or relative majority in each municipality will be the basis of work in the Working Group and will be subject only to amendments justified by the above-mentioned criteria." So what it's saying, do you agree, Mr. Okun, is this: It's making the nationalities the dominant criteria. It's introducing economic, geographical, and other criteria, whatever those might be, as subordinate criteria, and it is only where some adjustment is justified, according to those subordinate criteria, that there will be an amendment or an interference with the main criterion of nationality?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's basically correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my reading as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And so whether -- I say nationality. We're talking about the three nationalities with which we're familiar now, Muslims, Serbs, and Croats, so whether one puts the label "nationality" or "ethnicity" on it, that was the recognised dominant criterion for these purposes?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then the development of this process, the Cutileiro process, if I can call it that, well, it ran into the sand, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ultimately. The -- and in particular, the position was this, wasn't it: That Mr. Izetbegovic agreed to -- well, particularly the later one is important -- agreed to the Sarajevo statement of principles, on the 18th of March. It says at the very end of that document "As agreed by the leaders of SDA, SDS, and HDZ parties in the fifth round of talks on future constitutional arrangements." But subsequently, and not very long afterwards, he withdrew his support and agreement.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding. I was not present at this. What was normal for the leaders throughout the negotiations, that is, for the leaders of the three parties, the Muslims, Croats, and the Serbs, was to agree subject to their Assembly agreements. We've seen that with Dr. Karadzic many times, and the Croats the same, although I think Boban probably had more control than the other two. But it is correct to say that when he returned to -- or after he returned to Sarajevo from wherever this was actually physically agreed upon, that the President Izetbegovic withdrew his agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it was -- acknowledging the comment you just made about such agreements being subject to approval by the relevant Assemblies, in this particular case it wasn't that Mr. Izetbegovic went back and was then overridden by his Assembly, it was that Mr. Izetbegovic himself changed his view.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think both are true. I asked him about that. As I said, I did not participate in this meeting of 18 October. But subsequently, when I was with President Izetbegovic, I recall asking him, and what he told me was that when he returned to Sarajevo and spoke with other leaders of the Bosnian government, that they convinced him that his agreement had been unwise. That's what he said. Now, there were other theories. We don't know this. As far as I am concerned, we don't know for sure why this happened, what you've just described. I have seen in many journalistic accounts the report, which as far as I know is quite unsubstantiated but it's very widespread, that the American ambassador in Belgrade, Ambassador Zimmerman, convinced President Izetbegovic to withdraw his signature. I asked Zimmerman about that directly, and he said that was not true at all, that there was just no truth to that. But it appears in journalistic accounts, and even in accounts between hard covers. You know, journalists do reach for the hard covers and write books quite often. But in sum, I think we don't really know at this point. One could ask other individuals. Izetbegovic is dead, Zimmerman is dead. I suppose if one wanted to delve into this, one would wish to ask Mr. Ganic, Ejub Ganic, Haris Silajdzic, people who were the acknowledged Bosnian Muslim leaders. But the fact remains he changed his mind and he did withdraw his agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, so whatever the reasons, Mr. Okun, as you succinctly describe them, or the possibilities you've described, the theories that are out there in the world, the -- as you say, the fact is that Mr. Izetbegovic and his colleagues in the SDA did change their minds. That's an obvious fact.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was inevitably seen by the Bosnian Serbs as some sort of a -- some sort of a betrayal.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they certainly did not like it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because they had, as we explored a few minutes ago, they had gone into negotiations in a context which they didn't like in the first place, Bosnia and Herzegovina -- they didn't, in effect, like A(1) of the document, did they?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they were proceeding from an A(1) that they absolutely didn't like to see what they could wear --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- in the context of --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. They felt they had given something and that the other side had not reciprocated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they regard Mr. Izetbegovic as having, if you like, got the main -- in A(1), they regard Mr. Izetbegovic as having got the main thing he was looking for.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure they would go that far. You could ask Mr. Krajisnik his views. He would know better than I. But surely they felt that they had made some compromises and that he had not reciprocated by compromising to the degree they felt that he should have.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, certainly, even if they felt that he had come a decent way to compromise when the agreement was reached in Sarajevo, once he'd withdrawn it, your description would inevitably be their viewpoint, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. I mean, they had signed, the Croats had signed, and he signed and withdrew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is it correct, then: You've described how the ICFY, I think you've usefully described it as, the ICFY, the conferences in which you were involved then --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia. I grant you it's a mouthful. If you can come up with a better acronym, I would be welcome to hear it. But short of that, we must, I think, say International Conference on the Former Yugoslavia, or ICFY.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I don't know whether I heard ICFY from you or somebody else before, but it seems to do.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, that was the conference that began in September 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is the -- or I think you said August, August/September is not a big --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said September. I said September, because that's when it began. The London conference was August. I mean, again, the London conference led to the international conference, but the London conference had a beginning and an end in August. And the ICFY, which was established by the London conference, so it is a progenitor of the international conference. But as the diary makes very clear, it began in the first week of September 1992, immediately following on the London conference at the end of August 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And given that Mr. Izetbegovic's withdrawal of his agreement to the Sarajevo Agreement, that happened very quickly, within a week or two of his return after 18th of March. Well, say return, it was in Sarajevo. He didn't actually return anywhere.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It happened within two weeks anyway, surely, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So by the beginning of April, because we know that April was -- well, euphemistically, and I put it as neutrally as I can, April was an active month.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed it was an active month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Put it entirely neutrally.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's important to bear in mind what we know, and you're quite correct, April was active and I'm not going to go into it further, but it was on April 6th that the European Community recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the United States recognised one day later. So that was a very significant act because the state was -- after April 6, 7, Bosnia and Herzegovina was a recognised state by the EC and the United States and by most of the countries. Not every country in the world but most of the rest of the world recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina after April 6 and 7.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But without any offence to any country, most of the world that mattered for these purposes had recognised.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. China did not recognise for some time, but of course, you're quite right; in this context, China was not as relevant as the countries that did recognise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- is the position, then, that between the -- I used the phrase running into the sand, but between the collapse of Carrington, Cutileiro, all that had run into the sand. Between the end of March, then, 1992, and the London conference towards the end of August 1992, there were no overtly active diplomatic negotiations going on.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. They did continue. You're quite right to say they ran into the sand. They were declining in importance and agreement was not being reached. But the Conference on Yugoslavia met in Brussels in May. I mean the full conference. I attended it as an observer for the United Nations. It's in my diary notes. And Cutileiro stayed active working on the principles, the map, everything we have in front of us. He remained active until June. He's written a book about it, by the way. As far as I know, it's only available in Portuguese. I've read it. It's called The Life and Death of Others, [Portuguese phrase], and I suppose you can get it or should get it. It's his account of this period, Cutileiro's book. So the Conference on Yugoslavia, while it was grinding down and, as you say correctly, running into the sand, in a metaphor for lack of success, it did continue. It reached a very difficult moment in July, because in July the British ambassador to the United Nations rather unilaterally committed and got the Security Council of the United Nations to commit to certain actions, and this infuriated - and I use the word advisedly - the Secretary-General, Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali, who was openly extremely annoyed at the British ambassador's action. And so what one was seeing as the conference was running into the sands was mad feeling around, frustration that agreement had not been reached. By July, Sarajevo had been under shelling for three months. The city was being destroyed before their eyes. And so there was a good deal of emotion at that period. And it was, I believe, that contretemps in July between the British ambassador to the United Nations and the Secretary-General of the United Nations that led the British government to initially think about convening a conference to get the negotiations back on track, as it were, and that led to the London conference which followed the next month, in August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were there in Brussels, then, as an observer, as you say, in May 1992. Who were the main players, then, at that particular meeting in Brussels?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the usual cast of characters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Being?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just read my notes. You can see for yourself. They're all listed. I can't give them to you from memory, Mr. Stewart. They're all in the diary. I'd be happy to consult it for you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Don't worry, Mr. Okun. We won't take time on that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean to be cooperative, but I don't -- I mean, there were 50 or 60 people at the table. I can't remember, after 12 years, every individual, but the main people were there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, I do not have the impression that anyone in this courtroom thinks at this moment that you would not be cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So anyway -- well, you've corrected what I put to you about the lack of overt political negotiations, because it clearly wasn't a secret meeting in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't secret. And you are correct, Mr. Stewart, the process was grinding down and clearly not achieving a solution. But that was happening throughout May, June, and July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you -- things got revived or took on a different form, as you've described, in late August 1992 and then in September 1992, and cutting not an enormously long story, but cutting it fairly short anyway here, it led to the Vance-Owen plan in January 1993. Now, you said in your evidence earlier in this case that the result of this process, the result was that by the spring of 1993, the Bosnian Croats had completely accepted the Vance-Owen plan, in fact, they had accepted it from the beginning effectively, hadn't they, in Geneva?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were the first. The Muslim side, which was the Bosnian government, effectively, had accepted the plan in March 1993. You said: They had -- talking about the Muslims, the Bosnian government, as they were, that they had some reservations but they were not onerous. Could you just briefly indicate what their reservations were?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have them to memory. They were listed after their signature, so they're available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they're formal reservations?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you may call them reservations. President Izetbegovic, I believe, called them conditions. More or less the same thing. But they were not killer amendments, as we like to say in the United States.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I see. That clarifies it.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not vitiate the acceptance, but they were conditions, subject to, subject to, subject to. They were listed right after his signature, so they're available to the Court if you wish to read them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. Well, thank you, Mr. Okun. You clarified that you mean reservations in the sense of express reservations or qualifications to the document itself as opposed to reluctance. The -- but as far as the Bosnian Serbs were concerned, you stated in your evidence earlier that by April 1993, the only side that hadn't accepted the plan were the Bosnian Serbs, and there's an intensive effort, and then you -- the Greek government, actually, called a conference and then you said Dr. Karadzic signed for the Bosnian Serbs, subject to the approval of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, consistently with something you described a few minutes ago, that it was not uncommon for the people concerned to make such a reservation, make it subject to that.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He signed on May 2, 1993, in Athens, and it was very clear that he signed reluctantly. This was no secret. I've described in the diaries that Mr. Krajisnik and Koljevic looked as though they were about to weep. They were near tears after his signature. And Dr. Karadzic was extremely depressed. So there was no doubt that he was signing with great reluctance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the -- Dr. Karadzic was a not constant attender in the sense that he was at every single meeting, but for practical purposes we see Dr. Karadzic attending so many of the meetings you had that he could be regarded as a permanent presence.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's fair to describe him as the principal interlocutor for the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- and he had been engaged, had he, throughout that period of the summer of 1992, from when the Cutileiro plan, well, certainly began to get pretty buried in the sand, through to August, when there was the revival of the new form of negotiations. Dr. Karadzic remained involved, did he?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would assume so, yes. I wasn't directly involved. And as you say, the negotiations became even more intermittent than they had been as the effort was drawing to a close. But I think it's a fair assumption that Dr. Karadzic would have been involved, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a recollection -- of course, Mr. Okun, we accept completely that you don't come here armed with a total list in your head of everybody that attended all these meetings. That wouldn't be humanly realistic. But do you have a recollection of Mr. Krajisnik's participation in the -- I call them the revived process, from August 1992 through to the culmination with the Vance-Owen plan?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In terms of the number of times we would meet with the top Bosnian Serb leadership, the first place would be held, in quantity, by Dr. Karadzic, and I suppose, although I'm just guessing here, that probably we saw Koljevic at least as much or maybe a few more times than we saw Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps about the same. Again, I mention what I said at the very outset, that Karadzic and Koljevic both spoke excellent English, and that was clearly a factor. What was also noticeable was that, at the most important meetings after January of 1993, when the plan was put down, I mean after all the preliminary palaver was over, at the most important meetings, Mr. Krajisnik was always present, and not Koljevic. And we've already noted that when President Milosevic called Mr. Vance in April from Belgrade to New York to say that we have another round of talks and, you know, the Greeks were involved, and could Ambassador Okun come to Belgrade with lord Owen, because Mr. Vance could not - that conversation is in my diary notes - that he said: I've spoken to Karadzic and Krajisnik, and they are willing to do the following... So I think there's no question about the importance of these three gentlemen, and particularly about the duumvirate of Karadzic and Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just jogging back for one moment in time. The meeting back in December 1991, at that stage of the different diplomatic negotiations and discussions, Mr. Krajisnik had not appeared at all at that stage, had he?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Nor had Koljevic. Neither. It was in December of 1991 when there was no fighting in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Bosnia was at peace in December 1991. The only fighting in Yugoslavia, except for the informal fighting, but the only formal fighting was in Croatia. And it was in December 1991, December 2nd, as we've already established, that President Milosevic said to Secretary Vance and me, in answer to our question about Bosnia: You should talk to the Bosnian Serb leaders and start with Dr. Karadzic. And we went to see Dr. Karadzic that day, and the meeting is recorded in the diary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, it appears, and this is simply apparent from your notes, that Mr. Krajisnik was present at a meeting on the 18th of September, 1992. That's a meeting -- that's what your diary shows. After that, there were a number of -- there's a meeting the following day. We can -- if the 19th of September, but we can take it, can we, that meetings on the 18th and 19th of September are in effect one meeting spread over two days?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that's an incorrect conclusion to draw. Better to look at the subject matter of the meeting, Mr. Stewart. They might be the same. I mean, you might want to continue it -- to regard it as a continuation, but that would depend on what we discussed. If, for example, in one meeting one discusses the situation in Sarajevo for a couple of hours and then the next day you discuss the situation, let us say the ethnic cleansing in Zvornik, those I would consider two meetings. I think the subject matter really is the determinant rather than the chronology.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we can probably just all look at the notes of the meeting and form a view about whether it's one or two.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a major point. It's just that what counted in the meetings was what we were talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, anyway, Mr. Krajisnik was there on the 18th and 19th of September. And those -- actually, those were in Geneva. Well, that meeting or those meetings, depending which it is, took place in Geneva. The -- he was then -- and that was the -- would this accord with your recollection: That was the first time, first time you'd ever met Mr. Krajisnik, was it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I was in -- I was in Sarajevo in October 1991, when the Bosnian Serbs walked out of the Bosnian Assembly physically, and I saw people milling around. And it's possible we might have met then, but I don't think it's relevant, because we certainly didn't exchange any views of substance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, we wouldn't need to take issue over that. If you were in Sarajevo on that --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the notes would show at what meetings Mr. Krajisnik attended, and if that's the first time he's mentioned, that's the first meeting he attended.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it certainly is. It's on your notes of these meetings. It is the first time, 18th and 19th of September. And then the next time -- well, there's a reference to him on the 25th of November, 1992, but it doesn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Probably better to intervene at this time than later. But if we look at the notes from March 5th, 1992, we see a reference to a meeting with Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, and Ms. Plavsic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you. If that's what that shows, then that's what that shows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- well, in the sense, everything I put to you would be adjusted then, wouldn't it, Mr. Okun, if there was a meeting on the 5th of March at which you were both present, then subject to what you've said about Sarajevo in October 1991, that would have been your first meeting with Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the diaries indicate March 5, and I'll have it in front of me in a moment. Yes. In Sarajevo. I now see it. Page 104 of the diary. The number that the Court has put is R0163755, on the left-hand side. And this was Dr. Karadzic, a meeting with Mr. Krajisnik. Koljevic was not present. But Mrs. Plavsic was, Biljana Plavsic. So this was a meeting with the three.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, if I may interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So March would be the first meeting, apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You might not know, but this Chamber knows, and certainly Mr. Stewart knows, that he's under some time constraint. So if he would be very much interested to hear more about that meeting, he'll ask you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Subject to that -- thank you, Mr. Tieger. The next time we see Mr. Krajisnik appearing at one of your recorded meetings after September is the 3rd of January -- I beg your pardon, is the 4th of January, 1993. So -- and it was -- of course, it was in January of 1993 that you first managed to produce the plan which then was, over the course of the next two or three months, was signed up eventually?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. January began the most intensive and the most high-level series of meetings in the peace process. Plenary sessions were held with Milosevic, Cosic, Tudjman. Yes. So after January, the entire situation was elevated to the highest level, and that's when Mr. Krajisnik was in pretty constant attendance, at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said in your evidence that -- of course, before you -- or in the early stages, when you first met Mr. Krajisnik, "he was known to us" - I assume you mean Mr. Vance, yourself, and others in your team - "known to us by name and reputation, even before we met with him, because of his importance as a Bosnian Serb leader." What was known to you? Let me put it this way: On the footing that you first met him in March 1992, immediately before that, what was known by you about Mr. Krajisnik and his reputation?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was a Bosnian Serb leader, that he had been a leader in the Bosnian Assembly, that Sarajevo was his home town, that he was particularly interested in Sarajevo, that he was a man of substance, a man of weight, a man of importance. That was known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you received some sort of briefing on the people concerned?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would -- Dr. Karadzic would talk about his colleagues. The others would talk about him. This was an open process.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I wasn't implying anything sinister, I was simply asking whether you also, Mr. Vance and you, whether you also, in advance of meeting people, whether you received some sort of briefing on your side from --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall that. We discussed, of course, with Lord Carrington the people he had met. Naturally, we would hear his views on the people he was dealing with, which were always informative, quite important for us to hear from Carrington, from Cutileiro. But we never received any formal briefings, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you get some informal briefing from Mr. Cutileiro about Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by "informal briefing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I've just been talking about what you've been talking about yourself a moment ago, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You used the word "briefing" and I'm asking you what you mean by "briefing."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Okun, I'll take away the word "briefing" which perhaps has too much formality about it. When you said "We discussed, of course, with Lord Carrington the people he'd met, naturally we would hear his views on the people he was dealing with, which were always informative." Now, I don't know whether he ever dealt with Mr. Krajisnik but did you hear anything from Lord Carrington about Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So apart from what you've just told the Trial Chamber a few moments ago about what you knew about Mr. Krajisnik before you first met him, did you know any more than that about his position, his style, his --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we knew his positions. Of course we knew his positions. They're matters of public record. I mean, I know you're the Defence counsel. I've never laid eyes on you before three days ago, but I now know you are the Defence counsel. You know who I am. I mean, this is not a matter of difficulty to know that he was the chairman of the Bosnian Serb Assembly or the president. I've already stated what we knew of his official positions. There was no secret about that, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: I'm trying to understand, because I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. feel there might be some misunderstanding. From what I understand from Mr. Stewart's question at this moment is that whether you got any information as Mr. Krajisnik being a hesitant negotiator or someone very reliable or someone who would change his mind frequently, or whatever. These kind of -- is that the kind of information --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'm talking about anything to do -- I think I used the word "style" as a rather loose word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But anything to do with his political approach, his personality, his style, whether you knew any more than that, beyond -- of course you knew his positions, as you've rightly acknowledged.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew that he was a firm advocate of the Bosnian Serb position. I wouldn't go beyond that and try to overcharacterise it. We knew it was he who had signed the document to the JNA, asking for JNA "help," help in clearing the -- in defending the Serb people, which in effect meant clearing out the other people. We knew that because that was a public act and had happened already in December. So one knew certain actions. But I don't want to overcharacterise or mischaracterise what we knew about Mr. Krajisnik in March 1992. Of course, we got to know him much better after we sat for hours talking with him at the table. That, I think, goes without saying. One learns as one gets into these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, are we at the right point for a suitable break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are at the right point, if this is a suitable moment for you, Mr. Stewart. We will adjourn until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, you talked about the relative roles of Dr. Karadzic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Koljevic, in your earlier evidence, and how Mr. Koljevic played an increasingly lesser role as time went on. So is it -- it may be a rather crude analysis, but is it that just as Mr. Koljevic's role declined, in a reasonably balancing way, Mr. Krajisnik's role increased?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know -- I don't know that I'd be quite that schematic. All three were present, for example, in Athens, in May 1993, at the ultimate act, the day that Karadzic did sign. All three were there. But there were some very important meetings, really essential meetings, climactic meetings, one might say, where we had as our interlocutors Dr. Krajisnik and Mr. Karadzic and Koljevic was not present. I refer to the April meetings with Mr. Milosevic, that is to say the end of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've already described Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Krajisnik as being rather different personalities. That's a fair starting point, isn't it, Mr. Okun?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The -- is it right, in Mr. Krajisnik's case, that you got nothing like the ranting - and that was a word you used about Dr. Karadzic - you never had any ranting of that nature from Mr. Krajisnik, did you?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you say that he was a more mentally organised, to-the-point person than Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic was a very intelligent man. When he laid out a position carefully, it was done thoroughly. But his emotion frequently got in the way of his presentation, and that was never the case with Mr. Krajisnik. Mr. Krajisnik always maintained a serious demeanour. But I don't want to say that we did not take Dr. Karadzic seriously. One had to take him seriously. It's just that his mode of presentation was much more emotional than Dr. Karadzic or than Mr. Koljevic, for example. Everybody has his own style.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Krajisnik show concern in the course of your discussions for constitutional, legal, or procedural niceties?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say for the niceties in the sense that they can be interpreted -- I'm not saying that's your interpretation, Mr. Stewart; not at all, but he was not, as we say, nit-picking. He did show attention to the constitutional principles, say, of the Vance-Owen plan, which were very important to the Bosnian Serbs and were discussed at length and which he did not like at all, and which he made clear, but I would not characterise that as a nicety. Rather, it was to him, as indeed it was to the plan, it was an essential component of the plan, so a disagreement with the constitutional principles, let us say, on the issue of consensus voting, on would the Serbs -- would the Bosnian Serbs have a veto power over everything in the Bosnian Assembly? Yes, he took a strong position opposing that, but it was a position of principle, not a minor negotiating tactic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it was apparent, was it, as you were approaching finalisation of the Vance-Owen Plan, it was apparent, was it, that it would need to be carried back to the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said so. It was not an obvious thing to us. But once they said it, they said it. I must say that we regarded that position that it would be taken to the Assembly as a sign that it would be ultimately rejected, because we knew the position of the Bosnian Serb Assembly from their previous meetings. That is to say, by May 1993, we knew the position of the Bosnian Serb Assemblies. So that when Dr. Karadzic said that his signature was conditional on acceptance or ratification by the Bosnian Serb Assembly, it was a pretty safe assumption that they were going to reject it. And I so indicated in my diary. You'll find an entry which, if you wish, I can show you, but I shan't do it unless you ask, but I can show it to you, that at the time I expected it to be rejected. I wrote that entry in the diary. May I show it to you?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary. Thank you, Mr. Okun. Thank you for the offer.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. But the only reason I mention it is that it does not say "I expect the plan to be rejected," but rather, I chose and quoted a line of poetry that would indicate that. So that if you look at the entry, it isn't immediately apparent unless you know the poem and what I'm saying. But it was clear to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is your "Winter is a comin' in".

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, that's another one, that's your other line of poetry, adapted.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's an adapted one about winter, yes. No, what I wrote was, "Bred to a harder thing than triumph." That's the quote, which I'm sure you know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Okun.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And you know --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll decline to finish the whole thing off this morning, but ...

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, it is a line from a famous -- well-known poem by William Butler Yeats, and the title of the poem is "To a friend --" this is the title: "To a friend whose work was come to nothing." And after the Bosnian Serb signature and the statement, "We're taking it back to the Bosnian Serb Assembly," of which Dr. Krajisnik was the president, that made it abundantly clear to me that the work of the Vance-Owen conference had come to nothing, and I so indicated. I mention it because it was clear to us what was meant by, We will take the signature back to the Assembly. It was going to be defeated there. And it was. It was defeated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I -- I think the reference to the poem should enable us to identify the relevant passage, Mr. Okun, and I won't ask you to give us the author of "Summer is comin' in". But the ratification by the Assembly, that was, I think as you've described earlier in your evidence, that was normal, expected procedure, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not at all surprising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the -- did Mr. -- Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik themselves offer any expression of the likelihood or not of support and ratification by the Bosnian Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall them saying it expressly. They didn't have to say it. They knew and we knew it would be defeated there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was, wasn't it, if anybody was going to sell it, if that's one way of putting it, if anybody was going to sell it and get it through the Bosnian Serb Assembly, it was going to have to be Mr. Krajisnik, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that he would have been one of the most important people, but President Milosevic went to the Assembly, so one sees his importance. We know that. And the Greek Prime Minister, Prime Minister Mitsotakis, went to the Assembly session. But Mr. Krajisnik was in the chair, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you turned out to be right, in effect, Mr. Okun. But at the point where you were at the -- in the final stages of negotiation of the Vance-Owen Plan and the question of its approval by the Bosnian Serb Assembly was concerned, it was obviously valuable to have Mr. Krajisnik involved in your meetings at that stage, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And valuable in a way which had not applied in the earlier stages of the discussions, during the period in the last few months of 1992, when in fact he largely wasn't at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's true up to a point. He wasn't at the very earliest meeting, but he participated quite fully, again in a very important way, in the September to December period, and the diaries indicate that; his many interventions on Sarajevo, his discussions of the ethnic areas. That was clear. And then increasingly after January 1993, he was a full participant. So we knew his views. He had expressed them. He was quite well known to us. By May we had seen a great deal of Mr. Krajisnik and we'd seen him express his views across the table.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you -- you say, Mr. Okun, he participated quite fully in a very important way in the September to December period. During the September to December period, he was only present, according to your diaries, on the 18th and 19th of September.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they were very important interventions, Mr. Stewart. What he said was very important.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I beg your pardon, Mr. Okun. What I'm putting to you: He was -- well, what you're saying, what he said on the 18th and 19th of September was very important?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But otherwise, from September through to the end of December, he wasn't there at all?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew he was informed of the situation. He appeared immediately in January, when the principals met, when only the principals at the table met. So that we knew that his views were very important and had to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How -- just on a purely practical level, how hampered did Mr. Krajisnik appear to be, if at all, in his contributions to the discussion by virtue of the fact that he really did not speak English?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that affected him in any material way. There was an interpreter present for him, and occasionally the others who spoke excellent English would whisper in his ear simultaneously as we were talking. Buha would usually just whisper into his ear. So I think he had a simultaneous interpretation that was really quite adequate, probably as good as this Court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Do you mean there was an actual --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Buha would be sitting next to him, and whispering in his ear, say, as Mr. Vance spoke.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I see. So there wasn't a specific interpreter with that task who was present.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was after January. Excuse me. Yes. After January, when we met in plenary or in smaller session at the Palais de Nation, and that's where we met, we met in UN headquarters in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think some of your later notes record the presence of interpreters, but at the September 18th, 19th meeting or meetings, it was done, was it, by Mr. Buha?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was done by whoever was present at the table. Buha wasn't always there either, but whoever was present at the table. But to answer your question, Mr. Stewart, the question, as I understand it - and please correct me if I'm wrong - the question was: Was he adequately served? In other words, did he understand what was being said across the table? The answer to the question, did he understand what was being said across the table, the answer to that question is yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Mr. Buha actually speaks English to a serious level?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I've met and discussed matters with him in English. You'll see conversations with Buha and me, and those were held in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Okun, my question to you really was whether Mr. Krajisnik's participation, and I meant in the sense of active participation, was hampered, because he doesn't appear, for example, in the 18th and 19th of December -- the September, I beg your pardon, 18th, 19th September, 1992, there is no note made by you of his having spoken at all. Now, I want to be clear. I'm not suggesting these are longish meetings, I'm not suggesting the fact you don't note someone is speaking means they never said a single word, but as there is no note at all in your diary of Mr. Krajisnik speaking at either of those meetings, that does rather suggest that he didn't make a highly significant or pertinent contribution at any point.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik is a man of few words. He spoke much less than the extremely voluble Dr. Karadzic and he spoke less than the equally voluble but less emotional Nikola Koljevic. They spoke more. The word count will show that. He is a graver, more severe person in manner, very dignified, and spoke less. It was clear that he weighed his words with care. It was clear to us also that he meant what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we -- some of your earlier evidence covered and spoke about the six wartime goals of the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we can take them one by one in shorthand. Number one, as you described it, was to have their own state, Republika Srpska, juridical state was the phrase you used. Now, given that I think we can -- you probably would acknowledge that all sorts of difficult concepts involved in there being Republika Srpska as a separate state.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, do you agree that that itself raised various questions about what that exactly meant internationally, domestically?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the organisation of any state is a complex matter. But it was clear and it was so stated repeatedly by all of the Bosnian Serb leaders, that, as they would put it, "We will not live under Muslim rule. We want to have -- be ruled by our own people." That was the shorthand of it. I don't want to go into it further. I mean, you could read their constitution, but that was the essence of the position, was We will have our own state, we will make our own laws for our own people. That was the essence of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was, in the context in which they found themselves, that was a reasonable aim to have, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that everybody else felt it was an unreasonable aim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Everybody else being?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the negotiators, and certainly the Bosnian government. But the negotiators, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen did not find that a reasonable aim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The second wartime goal was that the state - because that proceeds from the first goal - the state was to have continuous territory and to be contiguous with Serbia, not chopped up into patches. Once you've got the first goal, the second goal is really, would you agree, it's a natural follow-on from the first goal, that that's what a group such as the Bosnian Serbs would be likely to seek?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They would be likely to seek it. It does not follow automatically, however, on the first date. If we recall that Pakistan was created, and there was a West Pakistan and an East Pakistan. And if you look at Azerbaijan, Azerbaijan has a serious exclave, surrounded by Turkey and Armenia. So there are examples. Before World War II, East Prussia was separated from the German Republic. The famous Polish corridor separated it. So it's not a complete situation. The United States today, Hawaii is thousands of miles away from the continental United States, but it's part of the United States. The same thing for Alaska; it's a thousand miles away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: So it's not -- all I'm saying, Mr. Stewart, I gathered you meant it was an automatic requirement that the state be the way they wished it to be, and my view is that it's not either automatic or necessary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Okun, of course it is accepted that there are countries with bits of their territory somewhere out at sea or somewhere else, even on some other continent. I've only got to glance at the Bench to be reminded of countries you can add to the list. But that's not what I was putting to you. Even though there may be countries in that position, it's nevertheless a natural follow-up from the first --

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Territorial continuity. Yes. Territorial continuity is accepted, I would say it is natural, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then so far as the third goal was concerned, the way you described this in your evidence was, third, to be ethnically pure Serb or overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb, as they could make it. And then you added on: Hence the ethnic cleansing. Well, if we leave -- it's not a small topic, Mr. Okun, after all, but if we leave the "hence the ethnic cleansing" on one side as your addendum, as a consequence of this, to be ethnically pure Serb or overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb, as they could make it, again, in the context of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which they didn't want, in a state in which they were in a minority, which was a problem for them, as they saw it very clearly, to be as overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb as they could make it was again an understandable aim, was it not?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I have to disagree with you there, Mr. Stewart, because the -- even if the aim were understandable in the abstract, the manner in which it was being carried out and the areas over which it was being carried out were real areas and involved the forcible expulsion and removal and killing of other peoples, of Muslims and Croats. And we were able to see that in the presentation of Mr. Krajisnik that was shown on the video, when he showed the battle lines, the lands held by the Serbs, and under it was the ethnic map. Now, we have an ethnic map here, and there are plenty of ethnic maps easily available, and one sees that the areas held by the Bosnian Serb army in 1972/3 -- excuse me. In 1992, 1993, 1994 were not congruent, in many serious respects, with the ethnic composition of the country on a pre-war map. So that while one may say, as a theoretical proposition, that it's nice to live in, you know, a country with your own people, that was not the situation that faced the Bosnian Serbs in the beginning of 1992. They made it that way, and it was also Dr. -- I should say that Mr. Krajisnik says this in his presentation, as we looked at it on the video. He states that this will be Serb territory and that there could be some enclaves of other peoples living in the territory. Well, an enclave is a very small area of one people, entirely surrounded by the bigger area of another people, in the way that Goa was a Portuguese enclave on the Indian continent. Those were Dr. Krajisnik words, which we just saw here in the courtroom. So to say, and I understand your view as a theoretical proposition, that it's nice to live with your own people, but that it becomes a very different matter when you have a very large area in which hundreds of thousands of people are inextricably intermingled and that you then go about creating, creating, this pure state through force and violence and expulsion, and other acts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I appreciate, Mr. Okun, the thrust of your evidence is that the two are not separated in the way you've described it. But if we take away any suggested illegal means of achieving that goal, the goal of wishing your state within a state, as it's likely to be, to be as overwhelmingly Bosnian Serb as they could make it is, in principle, an unobjectionable goal, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I say, as a theory, in the abstract, one can say that. But if one takes the position that words have some relationship to reality, that one must base words on reality and one must base outcomes on the reality, then it really was an unreasonable goal, Mr. Stewart, because it couldn't come about except by forcible means. So it's one thing to state the proposition as theory. You know, it's another thing to make it come to be the case. And this was frequently at issue, and we have examples of it, which I don't want to repeat and take the Court's time, but we've already discussed and heard examples. For example, very briefly, Dr. Karadzic saying there will be war in Macedonia for the same reason there is already going to be war in Bosnia. Well, it didn't happen in Macedonia because the Macedonian leadership didn't make it happen. Now, it did happen in Bosnia because the Bosnian Serb leadership made it happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fourth aim was to -- or fourth war goal was to have a special relationship with Yugoslavia or Serbia, as the case may be. That was a natural aim in the circumstances, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not find that unobjection -- I would not find that unnatural. It would depend, of course, on the degree of the special relationship, what exactly did it constitute. But the -- many states have special relationships with other states. Dual citizenship, for example, extradition treaties, preferential trade relations. So there are many special relationships.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And fifthly, a topic that's come up a lot, of course, is to divide Sarajevo into a Muslim and Bosnian Serb section. Now, whatever happened in Sarajevo, again, in principle, Mr. Okun, if that were the only way out of an intractable problem, division of Sarajevo into Muslim and Bosnian Serb sections also was not fundamentally an objectionable war aim, was it?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't agree with you there, Mr. Stewart, because the population, above all in Sarajevo, was inextricably linked. So there was no way that you could separate the peoples, except by force. Nor was there any great desire on the part of the people of Sarajevo to live apart. During the entire war, for example, during the entire months and months, years, of Bosnian Serb shelling of the city, there were many areas, indeed there were individual apartment buildings where there would be a Serb family on one floor and a Muslim family on the other. I was able to observe that myself during our visits. I could see no inclination on the part, or very little inclination, on the part of the citizenry of Sarajevo, regardless of whether they were Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Serb, to be divided into two cities, like East Berlin and West Berlin. But it was a constant refrain from the Bosnian Serb leadership. Yes, you're quite right. It was emphasised over and over again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when these negotiations began in August, September 1992, did Mr. Vance and you, did you have a view as to what would happen about Sarajevo? What should happen? Perhaps I'll put it that way. What the solution should be, as far as Sarajevo was concerned.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the situation in and around Sarajevo was known. The Serb population was large in the city, to be sure, much smaller than the Muslim, but it was a significant population. But the surrounding opstinas, the rural areas, Ilidza, for example, were Serb -- largely Serb populated. We recall, for example, that Dr. Karadzic and the other leaders made Pale their interim capital of the Bosnian Serb Republic during the conflict. In other words, they placed their capital next to Sarajevo. So it was of importance to them. But neither Mr. Vance nor I had a fixed and irrevocable view of the future of Sarajevo at the beginning of the negotiations, to answer your question specifically. But it is also fair to say that we did not envisage, and indeed would find it very hard to envisage, dividing the city a la Berlin or Nicosia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So what did you see -- that indicates what you didn't see as a solution, what you didn't see as something that would work. What it doesn't quite indicate, Mr. Okun, is how you did see it would work in the long run.

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, leave it alone. After all, the people -- this city had been at peace for decades, if not centuries. It was the capital of the republic. It was entirely peaceful. The Winter Olympics had been staged there a decade or so earlier. It was a peaceful city. It was rather like The Hague. So we saw no particular reason to disturb it any more than I see any reason to reorder the population of The Hague, for example. It really did not enter our minds that one would want to split a city which was at peace, where its inhabitants lived peacefully. Let me recall for you -- and this is relevant, Mr. Stewart. Let me recall for you that when it came time for the signature of the implementing accords of January 2, 1992, the cessation of hostilities that ended the war in Korea [sic], discussion was held at the highest levels: Where would the accord be signed? Bearing in mind it was essentially agreement between Serbia and Croatia. Well, if the decision was made, understandably, not to sign in Belgrade - the Croats wouldn't accept that. That would not be happy news for the Croatian side. Nor would the Serbian side wish to sign in Zagreb - that left, Podgorica, Skopje, and Ljubljana, and Sarajevo. And the decision was: Well, let us go to Sarajevo to sign it, because it is central. It's the middle, we can all get there comfortably, and it's a very peaceful place. It's entirely calm. So we will be able to sign in an atmosphere of tranquility. And therefore, the January 2, 1993 agreement, the cessation of hostilities that ended the fighting in Croatia, was signed in Sarajevo, and it was signed, I repeat, precisely because Sarajevo was at peace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you didn't see any problem emerging from the fact that if the first goal were achieved and there was a Republika Srpska as a state within a state - of course in practice, there was already for quite a long time - but that Sarajevo would be placed in the other part of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I believe I already indicated, we did not accept, never accepted the concept or the -- of Republika Srpska. The Vance-Owen Plan did not accept Republika Srpska. Indeed, Secretary Vance and Lord Owen would not receive letters written on stationery that had as the letterhead Republika Srpska. They did not accept it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the sixth war aim, which was a veto power over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but before we move too much further and pass the transcript --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it's about the date --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's actually about the substitution of the word --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Your testimony was, Mr. Okun, that the January 2nd of 1993 agreement, cessation of hostilities that ended the fighting in Croatia was signed in Sarajevo, as you said, then a still peaceful city. I may take it that you wanted to say 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. The correct date is January 2, 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then that's corrected.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. It's -- Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. The other minor matter I had in mind was a substitution, the inadvertent substitution of the word "Korea" for Croatia in referring to the cessation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Did I say "Korea"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that's what I understood and what appears in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, dear. How embarrassing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both short names, both starting with C. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no explanation for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought it was an extension of this whole issue which I had previously overlooked. But yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps thinking of -- not to go into it, but there are divided countries, you see. When one begins to think in terms of divisions, I suppose Korea creeps into the subconscious. Forgive me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Okun, and the sixth of the war goals, to have a veto power over any residual powers held by the central government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, again in the context of the other goals with the first aim of having a separate Republika Srpska -- given the position the Bosnian Serbs felt themselves in, this was a reasonably natural concomitant, wasn't it, of the other goals?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say, Mr. Stewart, that while it is possible to say that it is a reasonably natural concomitant, if the original goal is invalid and if it cannot happen except by force and violence, to say that something is a natural concomitant does put rather a positive gloss on it. If I may choose an unhappy example along your line of questioning, one could say that if you agree with the Nazis that Germany should be free of Jews, if you agree with that, well, then it's all right, it's a natural concomitant to take them out to Poland and gas them. But, you know, nobody would, I think in this courtroom, agree with that. So it's really a bit misleading, and I'm sure you don't mean it to be, but it does leave the impression that these actions were all logical, simple, normal courses of behaviour flowing from a reasonable position. In reality, they were actions taken consciously to create a new reality on the basis of force and violence. So I can't agree with your characterisation that this was a natural concomitant, because the end result was highly unnatural, and in this case, on the sixth war aim, namely, the veto power, it was tantamount, indeed would have meant the non-functioning of the Bosnian Republic. It would have involved the de facto disintegration of the Republic if one side that does not accept the Republic then has a veto power over all of the actions in the legislature, then there's no Republic. And we did hear Mr. Krajisnik, in the video which was shown to the Court an hour or so ago, we heard Mr. Krajisnik, in his first or second sentence, referring to "the former Bosnia and Herzegovina." You see, he does not accept the state. He does not accept the state of Bosnia. So that to describe this action as a natural concomitant, while that can pass grammatically, it involves the destruction of the state, the physical destruction, and that's what the other war aims were all about, and this put the final touch on the war aims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said -- in your evidence, you said the other parties had war aims as well. I don't want to devote a disproportionate amount of time to the other parties' war aims, but in summary, how would you have described the Muslim -- Bosnian Muslims' war aims in early 1992?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their goal was to have a state of Bosnia-Herzegovina within its current borders, internationally recognised. They wished the state to be unitary, in other words, that it should have a central government and then a whole series of other institutions, but not belonging to other entities. And they wished it to be a secular democratic state, based on one man, one vote. The Bosnian Croats' war aims were to, first, remove, as help, remove by vote in the referendum of February 29 and March 1, 1992, to vote for independence. So to remove Bosnia from what was left of Yugoslavia in March 1992. Second, to assist the Bosnian Muslims in fending off the Bosnian Serb army and to defend the areas where Bosnian Croat people lived. And third, and here they had a similarity to the Bosnian Serbs, to have a special relationship with Croatia and perhaps even join Croatia at some later date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you may recall, Mr. Okun, Mr. Izetbegovic having said, and I think it's a fairly well-known statement, at the end of February 1992, he said: "I would sacrifice peace for a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina, but for that peace in Bosnia-Herzegovina, I would not sacrifice sovereignty." Is that something that you recall?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall those exact words, but he was interested in the state being sovereign, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Expressed in those terms, as -- and I am quoting, though in English of course, but expressed in those terms, would you have regarded that at the time as a rather warlike declaration?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think one -- I would have, nor could anyone objectively characterise that as a war declaration, because he had no army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a warlike, warlike declaration?

utterances.speaker: HERBERT OKUN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see, a warlike declaration. I don't know. I don't really think so. I think he was expressing what any leader would say who is on the verge of leading a country to independence for the first time in its history, in fact, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a very special way of reminding the Presiding Judge that we are close to a quarter to 2.00, Mr. Stewart. I'll inquire what caused this. Others might say it is music, but I would say it is noise, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I thought it was a commercial break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is effective, although I'd like it not to be repeated. We are close to a quarter to 2.00. I would like to have one minute with the parties to discuss a few practical matters, but we are not going to bother you with that, Mr. Okun. We'd like to see you back tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom, and may I instruct you again not to speak with anyone about your testimony, whether given or still about to be given.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, to get a better impression of what our day will look like tomorrow, how much time would you think you still need for the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would expect to finish either within or for practical purposes close to within the first session --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then there might be some questions from the Bench. There might be some questions in redirect. So we'll certainly find tomorrow some remaining time for practical matters. I'd like to pay attention tomorrow both to the -- well, as it's sometimes said, the conditions or at least the monitoring of the Chamber, the plans made by the parties to expose them publicly and to see what further has to be said about it. The second issue I'd like to raise tomorrow is the statements and transcripts as far as tendering them into evidence is concerned. Because they, at this moment, do not appear on our list of exhibits. And we now are faced with the next problem, that the exhibits attached to them also do not appear on the list of exhibits. So, therefore, I'll make suggestions tomorrow how to deal with that in the near future. These are the two major issues on the agenda, but if the parties would like to add one, then either it could be just written down briefly in one or two lines and to be presented to the Chamber this afternoon so that we are aware of what the issues are. Or, if it could be said in one minute, fine, but otherwise the interpreters have -- we have stolen already time from them again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have anything right now, and I'm not aware we'll have anything, and if we do, we'll take up Your Honour's invitation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Same true for the Prosecution, I do understand, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 25th day of June 2004, at 9.00 a.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
